## IMPORTING LIBRARIES / PACKAGES

```{r}

library(tidyr)
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
```

```{r}

origfile_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/carolc57/Night_Hawks_Data607_Fall2026/refs/heads/main/gsearch_jobs.csv"


gsearch_jobs <- readr::read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/carolc57/Night_Hawks_Data607_Fall2026/refs/heads/main/clean_file.csv")


head(gsearch_jobs)
```

## Assessing Missing Values in location and description tokens

```{r}

gsearch_jobs %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(location, description_tokens),
      list(
        missing = ~sum(is.na(.)),
        percent_missing = ~round(mean(is.na(.)) * 100, 2)
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```

## Classifying Data-Related Job Categories

Job postings are classified into four categories: Data Engineer, Data Science, Data Analyst, and Other. The classification uses keywords found in job descriptions to identify the type of role.

```{r categorize jobs}
jobs <- jobs %>%
  mutate(
    job_cat = case_when(
      grepl("ETL|pipeline|warehouse|architect",
            description, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Data Engineer",
      
      grepl("machine learning|modeling|A/B testing",
            description, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Data Science",
      
      grepl("analyst",
            description, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Data Analyst",
      
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

```

## Distribution of Job Categories

```{r}
table(jobs$job_cat)
```

## Extracting City and State Information

Job postings located in the United States are filtered from the dataset to extract city and state from description. State abbreviations are then converted into their full state names.

```{r}
united_s <- gsearch_jobs %>%
  filter(grepl("United States", location, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    base_location = str_extract(description, "[A-Z][a-z]+, [A-Z]{2}|[A-Z][a-z]+, [A-Z][a-z]+"),
    base_location = str_extract(base_location, "[A-Z]{2}$"),
    base_location = state.name[match(base_location, state.abb)]
    )
```

```{r combine locations to jobs}
jobs <- jobs %>%
  left_join(
    united_s %>% select(index, base_location),
    by = "index"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    state_abbr = str_extract(
      location,
      regex("[A-Z]{2}$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    state_abbr = str_to_upper(state_abbr),
    base_location = coalesce(
      base_location,
      state.name[match(state_abbr, state.abb)]
    ),
    base_location = ifelse(
      is.na(base_location),
      "Remote/Hybrid",
      base_location
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-state_abbr, -location, -description, -via, -work_from_home)
```

## Distribution of Job Postings by State

The five states with the highest number of job postings are identified and displayed in a bar chart. Remote and hybrid postings are excluded from this comparison.

```{r}
top_5_states <- jobs %>%
  filter(base_location != "Remote/Hybrid", !is.na(base_location)) %>%
  count(base_location, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot(top_5_states, aes(x = reorder(base_location, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkolivegreen3") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 5 States by Job Postings",
    x = "State",
    y = "Number of Job Postings"
  )
```

## Combining Salary and Location Data

Standardized salary information is added to the job postings dataset by matching records using the job index. This allows salary information to be compared across job categories and locations.

```{r}
plot_data <- salary %>%
  select(index, salary_standardized) %>%
  left_join(
    jobs %>% select(index, base_location, job_cat),
    by = "index"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(plot_data %>%
         filter(
           !is.na(base_location),
           !is.na(job_cat),
           !is.na(salary_standardized)
         ) %>%
         group_by(base_location) %>%
         filter(n() >= 5) %>%
         ungroup(),
       aes(x = base_location,
           y = salary_standardized,
           fill = job_cat)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Salaries by Job Category and Location",
    x = "Location",
    y = "Average Salary",
    fill = "Job Category"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
```

## Soft Skills

Forbes.com (<https://www.forbes.com/advisor/business/soft-skills-examples/>) defines soft stills as "the characteristics and attributes that allown one person to interact with another person for a specific purpose. They differ from hard skills, which are technical and measurable.

While not explicitly identified as such in our sample, I studied the description column of the data set and observed a treasure trove of what we now understand are soft skills. These soft skills, are also known as transferable skills, are desirable traits that employers screen for. Thus, I parsed the description field of the jobs table for some common soft skills, grouping them by a common phrase into a new table entitled "softskills."

In the same Forbes.com article, entitled "10 Essential Soft Skills", Chris Coussons, founder and CEP of London-based digital markieting company Visionary Marketing, explains why he values his employees’ soft skills more than their technical and educational qualifications. “Technical skills might get someone through the door, but it’s their communication, empathy and willingness to learn that determine how well they work with others, handle pressure and adapt when things inevitably shift,” he states.

Thus we decided to include them in our evaluation of Data Science skills.

```{r}
softskills <- jobs |>
  transmute(
    Communication     = grepl("communicat", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Collaborative     = grepl("collaborat|group|team", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Confidence        = grepl("confiden", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Critical_analysis = grepl("critical", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Leadership        = grepl("leader", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Problem_solving   = grepl("problem solving", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Time_Mgmnt        = grepl("manage", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Visualization     = grepl("visualization", description, ignore.case = TRUE)
  )

softskills
```

```{r}
softskills_freq <- softskills |>
  select(-1) |>
  summarise_all(sum) |>
  gather(skill, freq) |>
  arrange(desc(freq))

softskills_freq
```

```{r softskills visualizaiton}
  ggplot(softskills_freq,aes(x=reorder(skill, freq), y=freq)) + geom_bar(stat='identity',fill="orange") + xlab('') + ylab('Frequency') + labs(title='Valued Soft Skills - All Jobs') + coord_flip()
  
  
```

#### Next we'll look at the top 5 in-demand soft skills for our job categories.

```{r Data analyst soft skills}
freq_softskills_analyst<- job_cat |>
  filter(new_title == 'Data Analyst') %>%

    Communication     = grepl("communicat", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Collaborative     = grepl("collaborat|group|team", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Confidence        = grepl("confiden", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Critical_analysis = grepl("critical", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Leadership        = grepl("leader", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Problem_solving   = grepl("problem solving", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Time_Mgmnt        = grepl("manage", description, ignore.case = TRUE),
    Visualization     = grepl("visualization", description, ignore.case = TRUE)

  tidyr::pivot_longer(
```

## CLEANING TABLES

```{r}

## CLEANING THE SALARY TABLE

## REMOVING UNWANTED COLUMNS

names(salary)

salary <- salary %>%
  dplyr::select(-`...1`, -salary_pay) ## removed the column labeled ...1 , salary_pay

names(salary)

head(salary)

## CLEANING JOB_SKILLS TABLE

## REMOVING UNWANTED COLUNMS

names(job_skills)

job_skills <- job_skills %>%
  dplyr::select(-`...1`) ## removed the column labeled ...1

head(job_skills)

## CLEANING THE WIDE DATA FORMAT 

names(job_skills)

job_skills_separated <- tidyr::separate_rows(
  job_skills,
  skill_name,
  sep = ","
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(skill_name = stringr::str_trim(skill_name)) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(skill_name), skill_name != "")

job_skills_separated

## CLEANING THE JOBS TABLE

## REMOVING UNWANTED COLUMNS

names(jobs)

jobs <- jobs %>%
  dplyr::select(-`...1`) ## removed the column labeled ...1

head(jobs)

## CLEANING THE JOB_EXTENSION TABLE

## REMOVING UNWANTED COLUMNS

names(job_extension)

job_extension <- job_extension %>%
  dplyr::select(-`...1`) ## removed the column labeled ...1

head(job_extension)

## PARSING OUT THE EXTENSION_TEXT

extension_long <- job_extension |>
  tidyr::separate_rows(extension_text, sep = "',\\s*'") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    extension_text = stringr::str_remove(extension_text, "^\\['"),
    extension_text = stringr::str_remove(extension_text, "'\\]$"),
    extension_text = stringr::str_trim(extension_text)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(extension_text), extension_text != "")

extension_long
```

## MERGING ALL FOUR TABLES

```{r}

names(jobs)
names(salary)
names(job_skills_separated)
names(extension_long)

valued_jobs <- jobs |>
  dplyr::left_join(salary, by = "index") |>
  dplyr::left_join(job_skills_separated, by = "index") |>
  dplyr::left_join(extension_long, by = "index")

head(valued_jobs)

names(valued_jobs)

```

## EXPLORATORY ANALYSIS - GROUP BY

```{r}

names(valued_jobs)
head(valued_jobs)

skill_summary <- valued_jobs %>%
  rename(
    skill = skill_name,
    salary = salary_standardized
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    skill_key = str_to_lower(str_trim(skill)),
    skill_group = case_when(
      skill_key %in% c("sql", "nosql","pl sql","t sql","postgresql  
","  mysql","mssql","postgres","postgresql","mysql","no sql","sql") ~ "sql",
      skill_key %in% c(
        "numpy", "pandas","matplotlib","matlab" ,"seaborn","matlab  
", "scipy", "scikit-learn",
        "sklearn", "pytorch", "tensorflow","jupyter","pyspark"
      ) ~ "python",
      skill_key %in% c("ggplot", "ggplot2", "dplyr") ~ "r",
      skill_key == "vba" ~ "excel",
      skill_key %in% c("dax", "powerbi", "power bi") ~ "power bi",
      TRUE ~ skill_key
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(skill_group), skill_group != "") %>%
  group_by(skill_group) %>%
  summarise(
    sum_salary = sum(salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_salary = mean(salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percent_contribution = 100 * sum_salary / sum(sum_salary)
  )



skill_summary

skill_summary <- skill_summary %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(skill_group), skill_group != "")


top_10_skills <- skill_summary %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(
    order_by = sum_salary,
    n = 10,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(sum_salary))

## ADDING SOME COMMAS AND RENAMING COLUMNS

top_10_skills <- top_10_skills %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    sum_salary = format(sum_salary, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE),
    average_salary = formatC(
      average_salary,
      format = "f",
      digits = 2,
      big.mark = ","
    ),
    percent_contribution = round(percent_contribution, 2)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::rename(`% contribution` = percent_contribution)

top_10_skills
```

## VISUALIZATION - TOP 10 SKILLS

```{r}

ggplot2::ggplot(
  top_10_skills,
  ggplot2::aes(
    x = reorder(skill_group, `% contribution`),
    y = `% contribution`
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "DarkGreen") +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Top 10 Hard Skills by Salary Contribution",
    x = "Hard Skill",
    y = "Salary contribution (%)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```
